title: Why Your Budget Dies in January (The Paycheck Method)

lines.say: If you've ever started a budget in January and quit by February,
it probably wasn't your fault.

scene.text: Most budgets are built for a life that doesn't exist.

lines.say: Most budgets are built for a life that doesn't exist.
One where you get paid once a month,
every bill is the same,
and nothing surprising ever happens.
So today I'll show you the paycheck method. A budget built around when your money actually arrives, using real numbers, start to finish.
First, why budgets break. There are three reasons.
Reason one. You budget by the month, but you get paid every two weeks.
Rent is due on the first. Your paycheck lands on the fifth.
So for a few days, a perfectly good monthly budget says you're fine, and your bank account says you're not.
Reason two. The surprise expenses aren't really surprises. Gifts, car registration, that subscription that renews every January.
They happen every single year. We just don't plan for them.
Reason three. The budget has no room to breathe. Cut every dollar of fun, and the first coffee you buy makes the whole thing feel broken.
So let's fix all three.
Here's our example. Take-home pay is eighteen hundred and fifty dollars, every two weeks.
Step one. List every bill with its due date, and give each bill to the paycheck that arrives before it.

lines.cap: Paycheck 1 covers rent, phone and the student loan: $1,585, leaving just $265.
lines.say: Paycheck one covers rent, phone, and the student loan. That's fifteen eighty-five, leaving just two sixty-five.

lines.cap: Paycheck 2 covers the car, internet, insurance, utilities and the card minimum: $786, leaving $1,064.
lines.say: Paycheck two covers the car, internet, insurance, utilities, and the credit card minimum. Seven eighty-six, leaving ten sixty-four.
See the problem? Half the month feels broke, and the other half feels rich. That's exactly when overspending happens.

lines.cap: The fix: move $400 from paycheck 2 into a buffer that pays part of next month's rent.
lines.say: The fix. Move four hundred dollars from paycheck two into a buffer that pays part of next month's rent.

lines.cap: Now both paychecks have about $665 left over.
lines.say: Now both paychecks have about six sixty-five left over. Same money, no more broke weeks.
Step two. Turn surprises into a bill.
Add up every irregular cost from last year.
Holidays and gifts, six hundred.
Car repairs, five hundred.
Medical copays, three hundred.
Registration, one eighty.
Annual subscriptions, one twenty.
That's seventeen hundred dollars a year.
Divide by twenty-six paychecks, and it's sixty-six dollars per check,

lines.cap: moved to a separate savings account the day you get paid.
lines.say: moved to a separate savings account the day you get paid.

scene.text: Next January, the gifts are already paid for.

lines.say: Next January, the gifts are already paid for.
Step three. Pick one fun number.

scene.foot: Spending it isn't failing. It's the plan.

lines.cap: Groceries and gas get $320 per paycheck.
lines.say: Groceries and gas get three twenty per paycheck.

lines.cap: Then $100 of fun money. No tracking, no guilt.
lines.say: Then a hundred dollars of fun money. No tracking, no guilt.
When it's gone, it's gone. But spending it isn't failing. It's the plan working.
Step four. Whatever's left gets one job.
Paycheck one. Six sixty-five, minus sixty-six, minus three twenty, minus a hundred.
One seventy-nine left. Paycheck two leaves one seventy-eight.

scene.label: Every month, pointed at one target

lines.cap: That's about $357 a month, pointed at one target: the credit card.
lines.say: That's about three fifty-seven a month, and all of it goes to one target. The credit card.

lines.cap: $3,200 at 24%. Paying a flat $96 minimum: 56 months and $2,126 in interest.
lines.say: Thirty-two hundred dollars, at twenty-four percent. Paying a flat ninety-six dollar minimum takes almost five years, and costs over two thousand dollars in interest.

lines.cap: Paying $453 a month: gone in 8 months, for $285 in interest.
lines.say: Paying four fifty-three a month, it's gone in eight months, for under three hundred in interest.

scene.text: Same income. Same bills. Different plan.

lines.say: Same income. Same bills. A different plan.

scene.label: Bonus: twice a year
scene.sub: in one month. Bills already covered.

lines.say: And here's a bonus. Paid every two weeks, you get twenty-six checks a year, so twice a year, a month has three paychecks. Your bills are already covered, so that whole check can go straight to your goal.

items: Give every bill a paycheck, then even them out

lines.say: So, recap.
Give every bill a paycheck, and even them out.
Turn surprises into a bill.
Pick one fun number.
And give the leftovers one job.
